note: Invented pilot histories for the Squadron Room. Every route below is a real way a man reached a fighter cockpit by the summer of 1940, and every school, unit and place named is real and was doing that job at that time. The men are invented. Tokens in {braces} are filled from the lists beside them, by a number made from the pilot's name, so the same man gets the same past every time. Read by Get-PilotBackground in BOB2_SquadronRoom.ps1.

pastime: He played rugby for the station when he could and cricket when he could not.
He had built wireless sets as a boy and still takes them to pieces.
He rode a second-hand motor cycle far too fast, by his own account.
He sang in the church choir until his voice broke and has not sung since.
He sailed a dinghy on the estuary every summer until the war stopped it.
He kept the scorebook for the village cricket club from the age of twelve.
He had never been abroad, and had been in an aeroplane exactly once before he joined, five shillings' worth with a flying circus.
He writes home every Sunday and says very little in the letters.
father: His father served in the infantry on the Western Front and does not speak of it.
His father was a railwayman and his mother kept a small shop.
His father, a schoolmaster, had hoped he would go to university.
His father was in the Royal Flying Corps as a mechanic in 1917, which is where the idea came from.
His father is a doctor in general practice; an elder brother is in the Navy.
His father farmed, and he grew up driving anything with an engine.
His father works in the shipyard. He is the first of the family to hold a pilot's brevet.

text: Born in {place} and educated at {school}. He left at sixteen and became {job}. {father}

He joined the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve in {joined} as an airman under training, pilot, and learned to fly at weekends and on summer camps with {erfts}, on Tiger Moths and later the Hart. Like every man in the Reserve he was called up on 1 September 1939, two days before war was declared, and spent the first months of it waiting for a course.

{itw} gave him drill and ground subjects. {sfts} gave him his wings, on {trainer}, and the rank of Sergeant with them. He converted to the {type} at {otu}: a fortnight, a handful of hours on type, and very little firing of the guns. {pastime}
Born in {place}. He sat the examination for an RAF aircraft apprenticeship at fifteen and went to No. 1 School of Technical Training at Halton, passing out three years later as a {trade}. {father}

He worked on the aeroplanes before he flew them. Recommended for pilot training from the ranks, as a few ex-apprentices were each year, he was accepted in {joined} and sent to {sfts}, where he earned his wings on {trainer}.
He knows what is under the cowling better than most of the officers and is listened to by the ground crew because of it. He converted to the {type} at {otu}. {pastime}
Born in {place} and educated at {pubschool}. {father}

He answered one of the Air Ministry's advertisements for short service commissions in {joined}: four years on the active list and six on the reserve. Ab initio flying was at a civil school under contract, {civschool}, then a fortnight of drill and uniform fitting at the RAF Depot, Uxbridge, where he was gazetted Acting Pilot Officer on probation.
He took his wings at {sfts} on {trainer}, and was posted to fighters. He converted to the {type} at {otu}. {pastime}
Born in {place} and educated at {pubschool}. {father}

He entered the Royal Air Force College, Cranwell, as a flight cadet in {joined}: a two year course, flying on the Tutor and the Hart, with as much time on the parade ground and the sports field as in the air. He passed out with a permanent commission, one of the last courses to complete the full peacetime syllabus before the College closed to cadets at the outbreak of war.
A regular officer among men who mostly are not, he is expected to know the book, and does. He converted to the {type} at {otu}. {pastime}
Born in {place} and educated at {pubschool}, and then at university, where he read for a degree he did not finish. {father}

He learned to fly with the University Air Squadron on Avro Tutors and was commissioned in the Volunteer Reserve in {joined}. Called up in September 1939, he went through {itw} and then {sfts}, taking his wings on {trainer}.
He converted to the {type} at {otu}. {pastime}

pastime: He skis well and says it is the same thing as flying, which nobody believes.
He plays the accordion, badly, and is asked to anyway.
He had never seen the sea until the Gruppe moved to the Channel coast.
He reads whatever he can find and is teased for it.
He was a keen footballer and still keeps goal for the Staffel.
He builds model aeroplanes from whatever wood the carpenters will give him.
He writes to his mother every week and to a girl in his home town rather less often than she would like.
father: His father served in the artillery from 1914 to 1918 and came home with a limp.
His father is a master baker; he was expected to take over the shop.
His father, a railway official, lost his savings in the inflation of 1923 and the family lived carefully ever after.
His father was an observer in a two-seater in 1917 and kept the photographs in a drawer.
His father is a schoolteacher in the town.
His father farmed a few hectares and did not see the point of aeroplanes.
His father died when he was small; he was brought up by his mother and an uncle.
war: He joined the Gruppe in time for the campaign in the West in May and June 1940 and flew over Belgium and northern France.
He reached the front too late for the fighting in France and has yet to fire his guns at anything but a target.
He flew in the campaign in the West in May and June 1940, mostly escort work, and came through it without a claim to his name.
He came to the Gruppe from the replacement pool in June 1940, as the fighting in France ended.

text: Born in {place}. He attended {school}, and then began {job}. {father}

Powered flying was forbidden to Germany when he was a boy, and like thousands of others he learned to fly in gliders, {glide}, working up through the A, B and C certificates. After his six months in the Reich Labour Service he was called up in {joined}, volunteered for the Luftwaffe and was accepted for aircrew.

Recruit training with a Fliegerausbildungsregiment came first, then {ab}, where he took the A and B licences on the Focke-Wulf Stieglitz, the Bücker Jungmann and the Arado 66. Selected for fighters, he went to {jfs} and flew the Arado 68 and the early Bf 109 before the E. He came to the front through the Ergänzungsjagdgruppe at Merseburg. {war} {pastime}
Born in {place}. He attended {gymnasium}. {father}

He learned to fly in gliders as a schoolboy, {glide}, as most of his generation of pilots did when powered flying was still forbidden to Germany. After labour service he entered the Luftwaffe in {joined} as a Fahnenjunker, an officer candidate, and was sent to {lks}: infantry drill, tactics, air law and flying training together, ending in the officer's examination and his pilot's badge.
He went on to {jfs} for the fighter course and was commissioned Leutnant. {war} {pastime}
Born in {place}. He attended {school}, and then began {job}. {father}

He learned to fly in gliders, {glide}, when powered flying was still forbidden to Germany. After labour service he was called up in {joined} and accepted by the Luftwaffe for aircrew: recruit training, then {ab} for the A and B licences.

The Zerstörer arm was given its pick of the fighter school output in those years, and he was picked. That meant a longer road than a single-seat man's: the C school for multi-engined aircraft, a blind flying course, and then the Zerstörerschule at Schleißheim, flying the Bf 110 with a wireless operator behind him for the first time. {war} {pastime}
Born in {place}. He attended {gymnasium}. {father}
A glider pilot as a schoolboy, {glide}, he entered the Luftwaffe in {joined} as an officer candidate after his labour service and trained at {lks}, leaving with his commission and his pilot's badge.

He asked for fighters and was given the Zerstörer, which in 1939 was the posting the fighter schools' best pupils were sent to. The C school for multi-engined aircraft and a blind flying course followed, then the Zerstörerschule at Schleißheim and the Bf 110. {war} {pastime}
Born in {place}. He attended {school}, and then began {radiojob}. {father}

Called up in {joined} after his labour service, he volunteered for flying duties and was trained as a wireless operator at {lns}: Morse at speed, the FuG 10 set, direction finding, and air gunnery with the MG 15 on a flexible mount.
He crewed up at the Zerstörerschule at Schleißheim. In a Bf 110 he faces backwards, works the radio, keeps the pilot's tail clear and has one rifle calibre machine gun to do it with. {pastime}
